note: What has been improved in the atlas, newest first, one plain headline each. Hand-written, because a changelog read off the commit log says what a developer did and not what a reader can now do. The home page shows the latest four and /whats-new/ shows all of them. Add an entry when a change a visitor can see goes live, not when it is merged. date is YYYY-MM-DD; href is a path inside the atlas (starting with /) or omitted.

entries.headline: My research no longer carries a "Written elsewhere" tab of one person's favour write-ups; it shows only the family you are working on.
My research now opens with a short introduction to the name: where it is counted, and whose flag flew there.
The Flags Atlas pages now use the same full page width as the rest of the site, with text kept to a readable line length.
The Places menu is short again: one row opens the hubs, instead of listing all 34.
Connection & Backup has real icons: browser, file, cloud and share on the four ways, and on the back-up, import, send and link buttons.
Who are you looking for? is simpler: write a few words, add a photo, and Claude reads it only when you press the button.
My research is titled with the family (My research: Anile), shows which research session it came from, and has Rename, Remove and Print / save as PDF.
The volume count is now an icon with Save, Read and Contrast. It pulses when there is news or the Atlas has grown.
The Local dot is now a save button beside Read and Contrast: orange and pulsing when saved only here, green when online.
Relatives from one village share one card, with only the wars of their own years, and nearby books if it has none.
The volume count now sits right of Local in the header, in short form (3.43M).
Add pictures to a story and press Read: what they say joins the story, and the pictures stay with it in this browser.
Views and Filters are now just icons on the search line. The funnel fills in colour when you have changed a filter.
Looking for someone? A story that gives his father and mother draws both on the tree, and no longer puts you in it.
One search box for a place, a surname or a family story, with live pills. No family is chosen for you in My research.
Their journey now shows each year's flag, epidemics, wars and famines nearby, who led, and how the names were written.
The home map now has Start with your story: type or drop a photo, watch the journey draw, then start the family.
Reading the record now opens with a guided walk-through: what you have, what you know, their journey, your first steps.
New: say who you are looking for in one sentence, then see their journey on the map and a plan of what to look at first.
My research is now in tabs and lists the GEDCOM fixes still to do; the Ask page on Reading the record is simpler.
Roots & Routes now keeps your last tree files in this browser only; reopen one with a click, or untick to keep nothing.
Documents you read now get an Atlas page: a grey map, who held each place, registers, sources and name variants.
Read forms and certificates as whole documents, compare them in a case file, and save it all with the pictures.
Your online copy now saves itself on every page, a few seconds after a change, with no button to press.
Record Reader takes up to four pictures, then hands the reading over as a PDF, a text file and a prompt.
Reading old records has its own button, and now tells the story of a line: the place, its flag, its volumes and a map.
One search finds a country's records, its flag history and its hub, and the places menu now holds the flags.
Draw several areas and save them as one named group, or save the map as a view. Both sit in Views beside the search box.
entries.tip: Views: your saved map views and named areas.

entries.headline: Your saved areas, views and the names of your GEDCOM files now travel with your research, in the file and the six words.
entries.tip: This card lists everything kept with your research.

entries.headline: Light and dark mode: the sun and moon button at the end of the menu switches, and the atlas remembers it.
Connection & Backup shows the days since your last sync and your last file backup, with the date.
Some What's new lines now take you to the exact button they describe and point at it with a speech bubble.
A My research switch colours the map by what you have researched, so you can see what is done. It now lives in Filters.
Draw a box or shape on the map to list the places, books and archives inside, coloured by your research, then add them.
entries.tip: Draw a box or a shape here, then see what lies inside it.

entries.headline: Colour the map by your research: researched, busy researching, on my list, not started. Switch it on in Filters.
entries.tip: Open Filters: My research is at the top.

entries.headline: The Filters button is bigger and its panel roomier, with clearer groups.
entries.tip: The Filters button, bigger, with a roomier panel.

entries.headline: About now holds the sources too, in a two-level menu; the volume count sits beside the logo.
entries.tip: Open About: What's new and The sources are here now.

entries.headline: Mass-mortality events are equal-size cards with a short line each; the play control is at the map's bottom left.
Home counts now include the 5,943 eras tracked, and flags agree: 211 countries, 34 hubs.
entries.tip: Open the volume count to see eras, flags and hubs.

entries.headline: Volumes are listed once per place, and the book list sits inside the FamilySearch column.
Connection & Backup page: green dot online, orange local, red offline, and a warning if changes sit unsaved a day.
entries.tip: Your connection and backup status, with days since the last sync.

entries.headline: Reloading a place link opens that place; each volume is listed once; My research uses the full width.
A What's new button in the header, one volumes pill that opens the inventory, and a phone layout that fits the screen.
A surname's origin is now one compact card, and the header shows a green Live or red Offline dot.
My research can now save a dated backup file, restore one, and share a pack of what you found with someone else.
Reading old records: look up a Latin word from a register, and decode a date like die 30 7bris 1671
Names: type your whole name (David Ivan Defranceski) and every part is searched at once, given names paired by language
Name pages: who carried the name, by century and state, from Wikidata (the dead only), piloted on 20 names
Archive lists: the access colour is now on the number and its map pin, with no dot line, and rows alternate in tint
Place panel: FamilySearch volumes join their column, every list folds, the header is one row and names whose finds
Names: a page for every given name, with where it is said to come from, and two sourced stories of names on the move
Sources: each country now has one sources page, and place pages link to it instead of repeating the list
Names: a spelling shows under every language that writes it; Croatian, Serbian and Slovene forms added
Given names: the catalogue grew from 89 to 630 names (5,323 forms in 49 languages), each form with its source
Place panel: one sources block with the verdict, your progress, your archives and everywhere else
Roots & Routes fix list: grouped by what to do, with the Atlas's records, rulers and flags under each row, and a PDF
Greenland: 18 parishes and 118 church-ledger volumes from the National Archives, with the ones held offline marked
Roots & Routes: animated views, where to look for what is missing, and the old name of each place (Fiume, Salisbury)
Say your name: every form of a given name or a surname, and which ones a register has shown
277 wars, uprisings and massacres of 20,000+ dead on the map, with sources and where to find their dead
Zimbabwe's flag history now shows the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, 1953 to 1963
Wars, famines, genocides and epidemics, from the Holocaust to the Croatian war, now list where to find their dead
994 record regions now show who held the ground, era by era, across Africa, Asia and beyond
Places outside a record region now show each era's leader and system
Surname spellings: one catalogue, with the evidence for each
The home page no longer freezes browsers: map layers load when you switch them on
Add a source: a tidier form, and a header button that no longer squashes
A new source: UK Genealogy Archives, with free census, parish-register and marriage transcripts
History: 94 more movements now go somewhere on the map
History on a phone: year and era share a row, and the search is slimmer
Mass mortality on the map: 75 epidemics, famines, massacres and sieges, with what the sources say
History: focus on one country and watch only its movements and the flags it flew
Full screen is a button on the map, under the zoom controls
